issues.legal_issue: A grant for suitable maintenance is obligatory for an eligible descendant of a former ruling chief who lost a land-revenue exemption, unless there is a good ground for refusing it.
material_facts: The claimants sought a money grant or pension for suitable maintenance after losing their land-revenue exemption.
They claimed to be descendants of former ruling chiefs.
The Government rejected their application, and the High Court treated the grant as entirely discretionary.
issues.conclusion: The Government does not have absolute discretion to refuse a grant to an eligible descendant of a former ruling chief. Once the required conditions are satisfied, it must make a grant unless there is a good ground for refusing it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(1)–(3) of the C.P. and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948, must be read as distinguishing general applications under subsection (2) from the special categories in subsection (3). The rules made under section 8, particularly the additional enquiries prescribed for descendants of former ruling chiefs, support that distinction. Although subsection (3) uses “may,” its purpose and the conditions imposed make the grant obligatory when those conditions are satisfied, subject to good grounds for refusal. The Court relied on Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes (11th ed., p. 231) for the principle that enabling words can carry compulsory force.

predicates.maintenance_grant_proceeding: The claimant sought a money grant or pension for suitable maintenance after being adversely affected by the withdrawal of a land-revenue exemption.
predicates.eligible_descendant: The claimant was a descendant of a former ruling chief and satisfied the applicable conditions for a maintenance grant.
predicates.no_good_ground_to_refuse: The Government had no good or reasonable ground for withholding the grant.

issues.definition: When a qualifying descendant applies for maintenance after losing a land-revenue exemption and there is no good ground for refusal, a grant must be made.

issues.legal_issue: The Government must decide a statutory maintenance-grant claim in a quasi-judicial manner, giving the claimant an opportunity to be heard and reasons for rejecting the claim.
material_facts: The claimants applied to the Government for a money grant or pension under the statutory scheme.
The Government rejected the application without recording reasons.
The claimants did not appear to have been heard.
The scheme barred a civil suit, and the claimants sought relief under Article 226 of the Constitution.
issues.conclusion: The Government’s rejection was invalid because it did not meet the elementary requirements of a quasi-judicial process. The order was set aside and the Government was directed to dispose of the claim in accordance with the Court’s observations.
issues.legal_principle: The duties arising from section 5 of the C.P. and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948, required the Government to act quasi-judicially when deciding the claim. The bar on civil suits under section 6 reinforced the need to give claimants an opportunity to state their case and to disclose reasons for rejection. The Court relied on Article 226 of the Constitution and M/s Hari Nagar Sugar Mills Ltd. v. Shyam Sunder Jhunjhunwala, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 339, for the requirement that reasons appear when the Government performs curial or quasi-judicial functions.

rule.if: statutory_claim_determination and civil_suit_barred and claimant_not_heard and reasons_not_disclosed

predicates.statutory_claim_determination: The Government decided a claimant’s application for a grant under a statutory scheme.
predicates.civil_suit_barred: The scheme barred a civil suit concerning the claim.
predicates.claimant_not_heard: The Government did not give the claimant an opportunity to state their case before deciding the claim.
predicates.reasons_not_disclosed: The Government did not disclose reasons for rejecting the claim.

issues.definition: When the Government decides a statutory claim that cannot be pursued by civil suit without hearing the claimant or disclosing reasons, its decision must be set aside.
